---
title: "mecompare"
subtitle: "Marginal effects and cross-model comparisons of effects in Stata"
---

`mecompare` calculates marginal effects and compares them across models. It 
implements the framework of Mize, Doan, and Long (2019): the models are combined 
using seemingly-unrelated estimation with [`suest2`](../suest2/index.html) so 
that the difference in marginal effects across models accounts for cross-model 
covariances of effects, even though the models were estimated separately.

Some examples of the cross-model comparisons `mecompare` can be used for are
effects across nested models (e.g., mediation and confounding), across
alternative predictors, across different outcomes, across different model types
(e.g., ordinal versus nominal), and across models fit to separate groups or
samples.

`mecompare` also calculates marginal effects within a single model and
automates comparisons among them. Some examples are comparing effect sizes
across predictors, tests of interaction (second differences), and the summary
measures of Mize and Han (2025): the ME inequality of a nominal predictor and
the Total ME across the categories of a multi-category outcome.

More generally, `mecompare` can be used for most any test of marginal effects
within or across models. Every marginal effect in its table is posted to `e(b)`
and `e(V)`, so custom tests -- any contrast, ratio, or joint test of the
marginal effects -- are accomplished with [`metest`](../metest/index.html).

## Installation

```stata
net install mecompare, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data") replace
```

`mecompare` requires [`suest2`](../suest2/index.html), which installs the
same way (`net install suest2, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data") replace`),
and it ships with [`metest`](../metest/index.html), which automates
non-standard tests of contrasts between rows of the `mecompare` table.


## Where to start

- [Getting started](getting-started.html) walks through one comparison and
  explains the table.
- [Options](options.html) goes through every option with an example of each
  and lists the [supported models](options.html#supported-models);
  [Plotting and tabulating results](plotting.html) covers `store()` with
  `coefplot` and `esttab`.
- The **Examples** in the sidebar are worked examples from the published
  papers: the cross-model comparisons of Mize, Doan, and Long (2019); the
  summary measures of Mize and Han (2025) -- effect sizes across predictors,
  ME inequalities, and Total MEs; and the marginal effects chapter of Mize and
  Han (forthcoming) -- MEMs, AMEs, MERs and ideal types, tests of
  interaction, and group comparisons. The **Interactions** pages reproduce
  the analyses of Mize (2019) on nonlinear interaction effects.
- [Examples from the help file](help-examples.html) runs the help file's
  examples in full, and the [help file](help.html) itself is on the site,
  rendered from the installed version (`help mecompare` in Stata).

## Citation

`mecompare` implements the methods proposed by Mize, Doan, and Long (2019). 
If you use `mecompare`, please cite:

> Mize, Trenton D., Long Doan, and J. Scott Long. 2019. "A General Framework
> for Comparing Predictions and Marginal Effects Across Models."
> *Sociological Methodology* 49(1): 152--189.
> <https://doi.org/10.1177/0081175019852763>

## Related commands

::: {.command-table}
| Command | What it does |
|:------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`suest2`](../suest2/index.html) | Combines separately estimated models so that quantities from different models can be tested against each other. The engine underneath cross-model comparisons for `mecompare`. |
| [`metest`](../metest/index.html) | Tests contrasts between rows of the tables produced by `mecompare`, `meinequality`, and `totalme` (or any posted `margins` results). |
| [`meinequality`](../meinequality/index.html) | Summarizes how unequal the marginal effects of a categorical predictor are across its categories. |
| [`totalme`](../totalme/index.html) | Summarizes a predictor's effect across all outcome categories of a multiple-outcome model in a single Total Marginal Effect. |
:::
